title: Gravity
lead: How much defensive attention players draw on and off the ball, on the perimeter and inside, and how rolls, pops and cuts pull help.

blocks.text: Gravity is the defensive attention a player draws. Following the NBA's Gravity stat, this tab splits it four ways, on or off the ball and on the perimeter or in the interior, and adds two closer looks.

items: **Gravity** = expected room minus actual room, in feet. Room is the distance to the nearest defender. Expected is the average for any attacker in the same situation and spot. Positive means defenders stayed closer than usual
**Perimeter** = more than 20 ft from the hoop, **interior** = 20 ft or less (the NBA's split)
**Spot-up gravity** looks only at shooters standing on the perimeter, away from the ball
**Run gravity** counts the extra defenders a roll, cut or pick-and-pop pulls toward the runner

items.label: Help pulled
items.sub: of runs drew a second defender within 8 ft

items: Room depends on the defense's scheme, the score and the other nine players as much as on the player
Frames within a possession are not independent, so frame counts overstate the sample
The NBA measures defensive pressure from its own model. This tab uses the simpler distance to the nearest defender
On the ball, perimeter: 155 minutes, average room 5.7 ft
On the ball, interior: 35 minutes, average room 3.6 ft
Off the ball, perimeter: 544 player-minutes, average room 8.6 ft
Off the ball, interior: 224 player-minutes, average room 5.0 ft

Marker's position toward the ball (0 = on his man, 1 = at the ball)
blocks.unit: of the way to the ball

items: **High-volume shooter** = 10+ season three-point attempts per 100 possessions, at or above the league percentage
**Some volume** = 5+ attempts per 100 possessions, or 10+ below the league percentage
**Rarely shoots threes** = under 5 attempts per 100 possessions
League three-point percentage is 35.1%. Each player's percentage is shrunk toward it with 100 attempts of prior weight
Spot-up frames are on the perimeter, 15+ ft from the ball and not just after his own screen. 172 players have 100 or more
High-volume shooters were guarded 0.40 ft tighter than a typical player in the same spot
Players with some volume were -0.25 ft and players who rarely shoot threes -0.24 ft (negative means looser)
Player by player, spot-up gravity barely tracks season shooting (correlation -0.02 with volume, 0.11 with percentage)
Several bigs who rarely shoot top the player list on 100-200 frames, probably because they stand on the perimeter just before screening or when trailing the play

items: These intervals treat frames as independent and are far too narrow. Read the direction, not the precision
**Roll** = the screener of a pick reaches 10 ft of the hoop, or gets 6 ft closer, within 2.5 s
**Pop** = the screener moves out instead, ending 16+ ft from the hoop (web/scripts/cuts.R). Pops are also drawn in the play viewer and listed in its Action filter
**Cut** = a basket cut, or a cut through an off-ball screen toward the hoop
**Help pulled** = a defender other than his own within 8 ft when the run ends

sections.title: What this shows and does not

items: It shows how much room players get by situation, spot and player, and how often rolls, pops and cuts pull help
Spot-up gravity lines up only weakly with season shooting (correlation -0.02 with volume, 0.11 with percentage), so it is not yet a clean shooting-threat measure
It does not separate the player from the defense's plan, and expected room ignores the defender's own role and the shot clock
Model room on spot, distance to the ball and the ball holder's threat, with a player effect shrunk toward his archetype
Replace nearest-defender distance with a pressure measure closer to the NBA's (how many defenders lean toward him, and how far)
Test whether higher-gravity lineups get better shots for the others
